job.style: a step-by-step explanation of a process

passage: In India, the Parliament is the supreme law-making body, consisting of the President, the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha. Citizens elect representatives to the Lok Sabha, while the Prime Minister is chosen by the majority party in this house, not directly by voters. Once a bill is introduced, it undergoes several stages of debate. The opposition plays a vital role by highlighting flaws and questioning policies, ensuring the government remains accountable rather than just blocking all work. While the Rajya Sabha is called the 'Upper House', the Lok Sabha holds more power in financial matters and final decision-making. After both houses pass a bill, it is sent to the President. The President acts as a constitutional head and typically grants assent to bills passed by Parliament, as they cannot simply reject a law based on personal disagreement. Finally, laws are not static; they evolve through public demand, social movements, and parliamentary debates, meaning the public plays a crucial role in initiating change. This democratic process ensures that laws reflect the needs of the people rather than just the government's own agenda.

items.evidence: Citizens elect representatives to the Lok Sabha, while the Prime Minister is chosen by the majority party in this house, not directly by voters.
items.q: Meena votes in a general election. How does her vote help decide the Prime Minister?
options: It chooses her MP, not the PM directly
It chooses the Prime Minister directly by name
It helps the President choose her MP
It chooses her Rajya Sabha member directly
items.explain: Voters elect Lok Sabha members; the majority party in that house then chooses the Prime Minister.

wrong.why: thinks citizens directly elect the Prime Minister
thinks the President chooses Lok Sabha members
thinks citizens directly vote for Rajya Sabha members

items.evidence: The opposition plays a vital role by highlighting flaws and questioning policies, ensuring the government remains accountable rather than just blocking all work.
items.q: Opposition MPs point out weaknesses in a new government bill. Why do they do this?
options: To keep the government answerable for its plans
To stop every piece of government work
To take over the Prime Minister's job
To end debate and vote on it at once
items.explain: The opposition questions policies and points out flaws so the government stays accountable, not to block everything.

wrong.why: thinks the opposition exists to block all work
thinks questioning the government means trying to replace it
thinks bills are voted on without discussion

items.evidence: While the Rajya Sabha is called the 'Upper House', the Lok Sabha holds more power in financial matters and final decision-making.
items.q: The two houses disagree about a money matter. Who will usually have the stronger say?
options: The Lok Sabha, though it is the lower house
The Rajya Sabha, because it is the Upper House
The President, who can reject what he dislikes
The Prime Minister, who alone brings such bills
items.explain: Despite the name 'Upper House' for Rajya Sabha, the Lok Sabha has more power over financial matters.

wrong.why: thinks the President can reject laws he dislikes
thinks only the Prime Minister brings bills

items.evidence: Finally, laws are not static; they evolve through public demand, social movements, and parliamentary debates, meaning the public plays a crucial role in initiating change.
items.q: Villagers protest for years asking for a clean water law. How might this affect lawmaking?
options: It may make Parliament debate a new law
It may matter only if the government wants it
It may annoy MPs but never shapes laws
It may make the President pass a law alone
items.explain: Laws change through public demand and social movements, so the public can start a change in law.

wrong.why: thinks only the government decides when laws change
thinks public protests play no role in lawmaking
thinks the President makes laws by himself
